Caffeine works primarily by blocking adenosine receptors, and also affects calcium signaling and phosphodiesterase activity [1] [2] [3].
At low to moderate doses, caffeine improves alertness, attention, and reaction time, while effects on memory and complex decision-making are less consistent [2].
Physical performance benefits appear at doses above about 200 mg [2].
Moderate intake appears safe and may offer some benefits, while excessive consumption can worsen anxiety, especially in those predisposed to anxiety disorders [3].
The evidence on depression is mixed, with some studies suggesting a possible protective effect of moderate intake and others finding no significant association [3].
Individual differences in caffeine metabolism and genetics substantially affect how people respond [3].

On appetite, caffeine taken before a meal may reduce short-term food intake, though coffee consumed hours before eating had minimal effect, and evidence on appetite hormones and perceptions was inconclusive [4].
Caffeine is also used in skincare products because it can penetrate the skin, act as an antioxidant, protect against UV damage, and stimulate hair growth [5].
It is used in anti-cellulite products because it breaks down fat in cells [5].
Concerns about caffeine include growing rates of abuse and dependence, and the review notes that even doses below the recognized toxic range could contribute to harm in some individuals [1].
